title: An Analytical Model of Compute-limited Multistage Training Pipelines
claim: A staged training procedure of pretraining, then SFT, then RL can be modeled analytically, and combining stages gives the best performance for a fixed compute budget.
layout: 2 panels: left-to-right stage flow with nested modules, right-hand plot
description: Panel (a) is a schematic of the multistage pipeline. A top row of three boxes runs left to right: gray Pretraining, pink SFT and green RL with bulk feedback. Each box has a compute label (C_PT, C_SFT, C_RL), and colored arrows join the boxes. Below, three columns show the matching network diagrams. The first is a linear autoencoder with signal and noise input segments, an encoder E and a decoder D. The second is a pink rounded box for SFT, with a student w, a teacher w*, and per-step feedback. The third is a green rounded box for RL, with the same networks but feedback from the whole episode. Trapezoids stand for linear layers. Panel (b) is a line plot titled 'Optimal Performance under fixed Compute'. It plots performance against compute in FLOPs on a log axis, with blue, green and pink curves and simulation dots. The blue curve (Pretrain + SFT + RL) is highest.
caption: (a) A Schematic of multistage training pipeline. Each solid trapezoid indicates a single linear neural network layer. Pretraining is a Linear Autoencoder (LAE) that approximately learns the principal subspace of data x ∼N(0, Σ), where Σ is equal to the identity apart from a noise subspace, with identity covariance scaled by ∆< 1. CPT is the compute allocated to pretraining. In the subsequent finetuning (SFT and RL), a teacher network w∗gives labels y∗from the signal subspace and it is used to train a student network w learning in the subspace of the LAE encoder projection with feedback. The student predicts label y using the effective features ˜x. Importantly, SFT is modelled by every observation at each t updating the student, while RL is modelled by bulk feedback through reward at the end of a ‘correct’ sequence through the entire t = 1, . . . , T episode. We denote the compute allocations to SFT and RL, CSFT and CRL respectively. (b) Optimal generalisation performance against total Compute flops under three protocols: SFT only, RL only, and SFT with RL. Compute is allocated as described in 5.1, parameters are set as in 5d.
abstract: Modern foundation models are trained through multiple stages, yet how these stages interact and how compute should be allocated across them remain poorly understood. We introduce an analytically tractable high-dimensional model combining unsupervised pretraining with a linear autoencoder, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with noisy stepwise labels, and reinforcement learning (RL) with sparse episodic rewards. Using random matrix theory and an operator-projection closure, we derive approximate low-dimensional learning dynamics that closely match simulations. We show that finite pretraining data imposes a representation-dependent performance limit, with Bayes classification error scaling as the inverse square root of the pretraining sample ratio, and observe the same exponent in asymptotic SFT and RL errors. Better pretraining also reduces sensitivity to noisy supervision. SFT initialization shortens the initial RL plateau induced by sparse rewards, an effect we also observe in OLMo-2 1B on GSM8K. Longer SFT warm starts additionally improve asymptotic RL performance. Optimizing compute across all three stages reveals that the optimal allocation depends on supervision quality and total budget, with a non-monotonic dependence of the RL compute share on budget. Finally, a complementary compositional model shows how RL selectively strengthens task-relevant pretrained skills while largely preserving unused skills. Together, these results identify mechanisms linking representation quality, feedback structure, and compute allocation in multistage training.
